Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import importlib.util
for m in ['pdfplumber','pypdf','fitz','pypdfium2','PIL']:
    print(m, bool(importlib.util.find_spec(m)))
from pypdf import PdfReader
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
print('Metadata:',r.metadata)
from pathlib import Path
p=Path('tmp/pdfs')
p.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
for i,page in enumerate(r.pages):
    (p/f'page-{i+1:02d}.txt').write_text(page.extract_text())
(p/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'=== PAGE {i+1} ===\\n'+page.extract_text() for i,page in enumerate(r.pages)))
print((p/'page-01.txt').read_text())
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a practical stitching problem: localized misalignment can spoil an otherwise acceptable seam. Selectively realigning problematic patches is a useful modular approach that can improve existing pipelines without retraining.

Table I reports consistent improvements in all four average seam metrics across four seam-cutting methods and three datasets totaling 79 image pairs. For example, on SEAGULL, Baseline+LPAM improves SSIM from 0.638 to 0.696 and PSNR from 26.20 to 28.31.

Figures 1 and 6 demonstrate visible repairs to structural discontinuities. The inherited boundary-label constraints provide a sensible mechanism for connecting replacement seams to the original seam, and the overview and pseudocode make the overall pipeline understandable.

The manuscript cites the reused methods and datasets, supplies a code/dataset link, and reports principal parameters and computing hardware. Section IV-D provides useful, concrete failure analysis that helps establish the method's operating limits.
weaknesses: The contribution's distinction and practical advantage over closely related methods remain insufficiently established. The paper already discusses seam-guided local alignment in SEAGULL [25] and dense-flow-based seam estimation [21], but Parallax and SEAGULL receive only a single qualitative comparison in Fig. 6, and [21] is not evaluated. Quantitative quality and runtime comparisons with these approaches would better establish the value of the proposed integration.

The central flow modification is inconsistently specified. Equation (4) applies f to a displacement vector, whereas Eq. (5) defines f using a normalized spatial coordinate. If the intended operation multiplies the flow by a coordinate-dependent sigmoid weight, that needs to be explicit. Patch padding, taper orientation, and handling overlapping repaired patches also need clarification to reproduce the method reliably.

The quantitative evaluation primarily measures agreement between image patches along the seam; Table II similarly measures inter-image agreement over the overlap. These are useful alignment proxies, but they do not establish preservation of geometry or perceptual quality throughout the final mosaic. An independent assessment of structural distortion and patch-boundary artifacts would strengthen the visual-quality claims beyond the selected examples.

The experiments establish the benefit of adding the complete module but do not isolate its main design choices. Figure 3 provides a useful single-example comparison of flow modification and sigmoid parameters, but dataset-level ablations of selective patch extraction, flow tapering, and patch extent are missing. Consequently, the necessity and robustness of the proposed choices remain unclear.

The detector can classify uniformly poor seams as acceptable because its threshold is relative to the mean error, and small patches can fail to reconcile alignment with smooth merging, as the authors acknowledge in Fig. 7. These limitations directly affect the targeted large-parallax setting. Their frequency and severity are not quantified, and the assertion that false-positive patches cannot yield inferior results is unsupported. All evaluations also use REW for initial alignment, leaving sensitivity to initial alignment quality untested.

The efficiency claim needs qualification. Table III reports approximately 7–10 seconds of additional LPAM processing, while several underlying seam cutters take only 3–9 seconds. For example, Quaternion on SEAGULL takes 3.51 seconds and LPAM adds 10.17 seconds. This may be a worthwhile quality tradeoff, but the paper provides neither a direct timing comparison with competing alignment approaches nor resolution-dependent scaling evidence.
